name: Citizens for a Free Kuwait

summary.text: Citizens for a Free Kuwait (CFK) was a group established after Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait to build American public support for military action. According to the PR Watch account by Stauber and Rampton, the Kuwaiti government agreed nine days after the invasion to fund the arrangement, channelled $11.9 million to CFK over six months against $17,861 from 78 individual donors, and $10.8 million of CFK's budget went to Hill & Knowlton in fees; documents filed with the Justice Department showed 119 Hill & Knowlton staff in 12 offices working the account. CFK's campaign included the October 10, 1990 testimony of a 15-year-old identified as Nayirah before the Congressional Human Rights Caucus, later identified as the Kuwaiti ambassador's daughter. The Hill & Knowlton file on this site holds the Nayirah record; this file holds the group's own structure and funding, including a contemporaneous denial by the group.

facts.claim: Stauber and Rampton write that the Kuwaiti government channelled $11.9 million to Citizens for a Free Kuwait over about six months beginning nine days after the invasion, that the group's only other funding was $17,861 from 78 individuals, and that virtually all of its budget, $10.8 million, went to Hill & Knowlton as fees.
facts.quote: Virtually all of CFK's budget -- $10.8 million -- went to Hill & Knowlton in the form of fees.

sources.publisher: PR Watch (Stauber and Rampton, Toxic Sludge Is Good for You, chapter 10)
sources.title: How PR Sold the War in the Persian Gulf

facts.claim: Documents filed with the U.S. Department of Justice under the Foreign Agents Registration Act showed that 119 Hill & Knowlton executives in 12 offices across the United States were overseeing the Kuwait account, according to Stauber and Rampton, whose notes cite an October 1991 O'Dwyer's FARA Report on the group's filing after a nine-month lag.
facts.quote: documents filed with the US Department of Justice showed that 119 H&K executives in 12 offices across the US were overseeing the Kuwait account

sources.publisher: PR Watch (Stauber and Rampton, Toxic Sludge Is Good for You, chapter 10)
sources.title: How PR Sold the War in the Persian Gulf

facts.claim: On October 10, 1990 a 15-year-old identified only as Nayirah testified before the Congressional Human Rights Caucus that she had seen Iraqi soldiers take babies from incubators; a Hill & Knowlton vice president helped organize the hearing, and in January 1992 she was identified as the daughter of Kuwait's ambassador to the United States, Saud Nasir al-Sabah.
facts.quote: a vice president of Hill and Knowlton helped organize the congressional hearings

facts.claim: A contemporaneous statement attributed to Citizens for a Free Kuwait, reproduced in a collection on the Free Kuwait campaign, said the group had nothing to do with Hill & Knowlton, received no money from the Kuwaiti government, had offices and equipment supplied by the Kuwait Investment Office, and was financed mostly by donations; this conflicts with the funding account above, and the FARA filings themselves have not been compared against either.
facts.quote: received no money from the Kuwaiti government, and that the Kuwait Investment Office supplied offices and equipment
